Security.title: Security Zone
Security.description: Home turf for an Information Security major: a learning path, practice platforms, and fun crypto tools.
Security.toolsNote: Everything runs locally in your browser — no data is uploaded.
Security.caesarHint: The oldest cipher: shift every letter by an offset
Security.base64Hint: The most common mini-challenge in CTFs
Security.sha256Hint: One-way digest, used for integrity checks
Security.toolsNote: Tools are neutral technology — use them only in authorized environments: CTFs, labs, your own VMs.
Security.sqlHint: This is a 'vulnerable' login form: your input is concatenated straight into the SQL query. Click a payload button and watch how the query gets rewritten.
Security.sqlSuccess: Injection successful! '1'='1' is always true — the password check is bypassed and you're in
Security.sqlFail: Login failed: wrong username or password
Security.sqlNote: Why it works: the app concatenates user input directly into SQL — the quote closes the string early, and the rest is executed as code. The fix: parameterized/prepared statements, which treat input as data, not code. Every web vulnerability shares this root cause: trusting input that shouldn't be trusted.

Physics.title: Physics Zone
Physics.description: Physics × engineering: how electric motors turn electricity into rotation — brushed, brushless, brands, and interactive animations.
Physics.simsNote: Watch motors spin, and set the speed yourself.
Physics.brushedHint: Watch closely: the current direction flips every half turn (commutation)
Physics.brushlessHint: Three phases energize in sequence, creating a rotating field that drags the rotor
Physics.brushedNote: The split copper ring on the rotor is the commutator: every half turn the brushes flip the coil current, keeping torque in one direction.
Physics.brushlessNote: The yellow arrow is the rotating magnetic field: phases A→C→B energize in sequence. Synchronous speed n = 60f/p — vary the frequency and you vary the speed. That's a VFD.

Cars.title: Car Zone
Cars.description: Notes from a car enthusiast: engines, gearboxes, drivetrains, new energy — everything that makes a car go, and go well.
Cars.simsNote: Drag, tap and watch the physics come alive.
Cars.engineHint: Intake → compression → power → exhaust: two crank revolutions per cycle
Cars.gearHint: Pick a gear, set the revs, see how road speed changes (typical family-car numbers)
Cars.gearNote: Higher gears mean lower ratios: at the same revs the wheels spin faster, but with less force — low gears for hills, high gears for cruising.
Cars.accelHint: Enter power and weight to estimate the sprint (empirical formula, for reference only)
Cars.accelNote: Real results also depend on gearbox, tires, surface and temperature. Power-to-weight is the fastest predictor of performance.
Cars.fuelHint: Work out your monthly fuel bill
Cars.fuelNote: For an EV, swap consumption for kWh/100km and the price for per-kWh electricity.
Cars.suspensionHint: Adjust damping, then hit a speed bump and watch the body react
Cars.suspensionSoftNote: Soft damping: the body floats and wallows — bumps are absorbed but oscillations linger
Cars.suspensionHardNote: Firm damping: bumps feel crisp but the body settles fast
Cars.suspensionExplain: Green is the spring (stores energy), yellow the damper (dissipates it). More damping burns the spring's energy faster — less body motion, but bumps feel more direct.
Cars.batteryHint: Simulate a minute of driving: watch energy drain and come back
Cars.batteryNote: Accelerating drains the battery; coasting and braking run the motor as a generator and put energy back — regenerative braking recovers kinetic energy that would otherwise become heat.
Cars.vvtHint: Drag the slider to change valve overlap and watch the lift curves move
Cars.vvtLowSpeed: Small overlap: smooth and efficient at low rpm
Cars.vvtHighSpeed: Large overlap: better scavenging and more power at high rpm
Cars.vvtExplain: Overlap is the window where the intake is already open while the exhaust is still closing. Too much at low rpm backflows exhaust gas; too little at high rpm starves the intake — VVT gives you both.
Cars.turboHint: Floor it, rev it up — watch boost build and turbo lag in action
Cars.turboLag: Floor it at low rpm and boost doesn't come instantly — that's turbo lag
Cars.aeroHint: Drag the speed slider: double the speed, quadruple the drag
Cars.aeroNote: Drag ∝ speed²: at 120 km/h drag is ~2.25× the drag at 80 km/h — that's why highway fuel use climbs. A slippery shape (low Cd) saves real fuel.
Cars.brakeHint: Speed and surface decide everything: how far do you slide from brake pedal to stop?
Cars.brakeNote: Total stop = reaction distance + braking distance. Ice has about a quarter of dry asphalt's friction — at 50 km/h you can slide 60+ meters, which is why winter speeds must drop.
Cars.dynoHint: Naturally aspirated vs turbocharged: very different curve shapes
Cars.dynoNote: NA torque looks like a mountain peak (max around 4000-5000 rpm); turbo torque looks like a plateau (flat from 1500-4500 rpm) — that's why turbo cars feel strong at low revs.
Cars.steeringHint: Turn the wheel, change the speed: watch wheel angle, turning radius and lateral g
Cars.steeringNote: Turning radius R = wheelbase ÷ tan(wheel angle). Tires start to slide past ~0.8 g lateral — double the speed and cornering force quadruples. That's why you brake before the corner.
Cars.awdHint: Switch drivetrain, surface and throttle — watch how torque splits and who slips
Cars.awdNote: Under acceleration, weight shifts rearward and rear grip improves. A FWD car at full throttle on wet roads can exceed front grip and spin its wheels; AWD splits the torque so every wheel works less. But AWD helps acceleration grip only — braking distance doesn't care which wheels are driven.
Cars.crashHint: Speed decides survival: pick a speed, hit the wall, see how brutal the energy gets
Cars.crashSurvive1: ✅ Seatbelt + airbags can protect you — likely fine
Cars.crashSurvive2: ⚠️ Serious injury risk — the cabin is struggling
Cars.crashSurvive3: ❌ Likely fatal — this is why speed limits exist
Cars.crashNote: Energy scales with the square of speed: a 100 km/h crash carries 4× the energy of 50 km/h. Crumple zones absorb energy by crushing, reducing occupant deceleration into the survivable range — a car that 'destroys itself' is protecting you.

Challenge.title: Mini CTF Challenge
Challenge.description: 3 flags are hidden somewhere on this site. Find them and enter them below.
Challenge.level1Hint: No tools needed. Right-click the page and check "View page source".
Challenge.level2Hint: Press F12, open the Console tab.
Challenge.level3Hint: Open DevTools' Network tab, reload, and inspect the response headers of /challenge. Or try curl -I.
Challenge.level4Hint: The source contains a string that looks like gibberish — it ends with =. Decode it with the Base64 tool in the Security Zone.
Challenge.level5Hint: This note was encrypted by Caesar himself: every letter shifted by 3. Restore it with the Caesar tool in the Security Zone.
Challenge.level6Hint: Websites are more than HTML. Check the source of the site icon (icon.svg).
Challenge.congrats: 🎉 All three found! You may now call yourself Mayor of CTF Beginner Village.
